799.title: Broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13)
799.hook: they left the fountain of living waters for cisterns that hold no water
799.howItsDone: Jeremiah 2, with its broken cisterns, is read in synagogue as a haftarah in the summer weeks before Tisha b'Av, when the Prophets' words of warning are read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a plain almond branch, shaked, turned out to mean watching: look twice, and really see. Today, Jeremiah's first great complaint, and it's about water.

In a dry land, rain doesn't fall all year. So people dug cisterns: pits cut into the rock to catch the rain and keep it for the dry months. A good cistern is a lifeline. A cracked one is worse than none, because you only find out when you lower the bucket and it comes up empty. Now set a spring next to that, water rising out of the ground on its own, cold and moving, free for anyone. Jeremiah puts the two side by side, in a single verse.
screen: `A PIT CUT INTO ROCK.` → `THE BUCKET COMES UP EMPTY.` → `A SPRING, FREE FOR ANYONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is. "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water." Two evils, and they're a pair: leaving the spring, and then the digging. Hewing a cistern out of rock is hard labor. The people aren't lazy in this picture; they're exhausted, working hard on something that leaks. Living water, in Hebrew mayim chayim, means water that moves, from a spring or a stream, not water that sits. In this verse, God is that spring. The broken cisterns, in the chapter around it, are the other gods and the foreign powers the people chased, even going to Egypt and Assyria to drink their rivers' water. Earlier, God asks whether any nation has ever changed its gods, and says my people have changed their glory for what doesn't profit. A cistern isn't bad in itself. The Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, praises a great student, Rabbi Eliezer, as a plastered cistern that never loses a drop: someone who keeps everything he learns. The trouble isn't storing water. It's trading a spring for a container, and then a container that cracks. The rabbis also compared the words of Torah to water, reading Isaiah's call to everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters as an invitation to learn. So the verse leaves a practical question: what am I working hard to fill that never stays full?
screen: `TWO EVILS, A PAIR.` · then, large: `THE FOUNTAIN OF LIVING WATERS.` · then: `A CISTERN THAT KEEPS EVERY DROP.` · `WHAT NEVER STAYS FULL?`

segments.voice: Look back over the last week and find one place your time and effort poured in and drained right out: an app you refresh, an argument you keep rehearsing, a purchase that was supposed to fix something. No need to judge yourself; just see it clearly, the way you'd see a crack in a bucket. Then picture one living thing that could take its place: a walk, a call, a page of learning.
Broken cisterns. Pits dug with great effort that can hold no water, set beside the spring the people walked away from. Today's word.

800.title: Is there no balm? (Jeremiah 8:22)
800.hook: "Is there no balm in Gilead?" the prophet weeps for his people's hurt
800.carry: he stays, and he hurts with them
800.howItsDone: Jeremiah 8 and 9 are read in synagogue as the haftarah on the morning of Tisha b'Av, the fast day of mourning, when Lamentations is also read aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people left a flowing spring for broken cisterns that leak: a spring, free for anyone. Today the prophet who warned them starts to weep for them.

"Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?" To hear the sting in that question, you need to know what Gilead meant. In Genesis, Joseph's brothers, about to sell him, look up and see a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going down to Egypt. In that story, Gilead is where the balm comes from. So Jeremiah's question is like standing in a pharmacy and asking: is there no medicine here? Of course there is. That's what makes it hurt.
screen: `IS THERE NO BALM IN GILEAD?` → `A CARAVAN FROM GILEAD.` → `MEDICINE IN THE PHARMACY.`

segments.voice: Listen to the verses just before. "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." The season for gathering has come and gone, and nothing was gathered in. Then Jeremiah's own voice breaks through: "For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt." This is the man who has spent chapter after chapter warning, accusing, calling the people back from broken cisterns. Here he isn't standing above them. Their wound is his wound. Then the question: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?" The question doesn't doubt that healing exists. The balm is real; the physician is there. What baffles him is the gap between the cure and the patient. And the verse doesn't answer. Right after it, Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, so he could weep day and night for his people. Tradition says Jeremiah also wrote the book of Lamentations, and the Talmud records that view. Whether or not you read it that way, here is a prophet whose anger and grief live in the same chest. There is a particular pain in watching help exist and still not reach: the friend who won't call the doctor, the family that won't talk. Jeremiah doesn't fix it. He stays, and he hurts with them.
screen: `THE HARVEST IS PAST.` · then, large: `FOR THE HURT OF MY PEOPLE AM I HURT.` · then: `THE CURE IS REAL. WHY NO HEALING?` · `ANGER AND GRIEF IN ONE CHEST.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who is in pain right now, in body or in spirit, someone help hasn't reached yet. Don't try to solve it; just let their hurt sit next to you for a moment, the way Jeremiah let his people's hurt be his own. Then picture one small act of care that could carry a little balm the last few steps: a message, a meal, a ride to an appointment.
Tsori. Hebrew for balm: Jeremiah's cry that the cure is in Gilead, so why are my people not healed? Today's word.
Your line: he stays, and he hurts with them. Sometimes presence is the balm. Eight hundred days now.

801.title: Glory in kindness (Jeremiah 9:22–23)
801.hook: let no one glory in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the God of kindness and justice
801.carry: here, in kitchens and courts and streets
801.howItsDone: These verses close the haftarah read in synagogue on the morning of Tisha b'Av, so the day of mourning's reading from the Prophets ends on kindness, justice and righteousness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah asked why there was no healing with tsori, the balm, right there in Gilead: he stays, and he hurts with them. Today, a few verses on, the same prophet talks about bragging.
screen: `HE STAYS, AND HE HURTS WITH THEM.`

segments.voice: Scroll any feed for a minute and the boasts sort themselves into three piles. Look how smart I am: the degree, the hot take, the clever reply. Look how strong I am: the workout, the win, the promotion. Look how much I have: the car, the kitchen, the trip. The piles have changed their clothes over the centuries, but not their shape. Jeremiah names all three in one breath, and then tells you the one thing worth boasting about. It isn't any of them.
screen: `SMART, STRONG, RICH.` → `THE BOASTS HAVEN'T CHANGED.` → `ONE THING WORTH BOASTING ABOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. "Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches." Wisdom, might, riches: the three piles. The verse doesn't say they're bad. Being wise is good; strength is useful; money can do a lot. They're just not what to glory in. Then the turn. "But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD." Three Hebrew words: chesed, kindness; mishpat, justice; tzedakah, righteousness. Three boasts out; three of God's ways in. And look at the strange shape of the boast. It isn't I am kind. It's I know a God who does kindness. To know God, in this verse, is to understand what God does and delights in. And where? In the earth: not only in heaven, but here, in kitchens and courts and streets. In the last chapter of his Guide for the Perplexed, the philosopher Maimonides turns to this very verse. His reading, in brief: knowing God leads somewhere practical, to acting with kindness, justice and righteousness yourself. So a ban on bragging becomes a job description, and that knowing is meant to show in the hands.
screen: `NOT WISDOM, NOT MIGHT, NOT RICHES.` · then, large: `KINDNESS, JUSTICE, RIGHTEOUSNESS.` · then: `IN THE EARTH.` · `MAIMONIDES' LAST CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last few days and find one moment of kindness you saw, or were given, or managed to give: someone held a door, covered a shift, said the right word. Hold it for a moment, and let it be the thing that matters about your week. If you pray, you can hold Jeremiah's words: for in these things I delight.
Chesed. Hebrew for kindness: not in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the God who does kindness, justice and righteousness in the earth. Today's word.
Your line: here, in kitchens and courts and streets. The one boast left is knowing the God who delights in kindness. See you at the potter's house.

802.title: The potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1–6)
802.hook: clay spoiled on the wheel is shaped again
802.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur evening, Ashkenazi prayer books include the liturgical poem Ki hineh kachomer, behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, which takes its image from Jeremiah 18.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah set aside wisdom, might and riches as things to brag about, and kept chesed, kindness: here, in kitchens and courts and streets. Today, the prophet goes to work, in someone else's workshop.
screen: `HERE, IN KITCHENS AND COURTS AND STREETS.`

segments.voice: "Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words." This time the message doesn't come in a vision or a dream. Jeremiah is sent on an errand, down to a workshop. There's the potter, working a lump of clay at the wheel. Wet hands, a turning wheel, a pot rising. And then, halfway up, something goes wrong: a wobble, a slump, a wall caving in. What the potter does next is the whole lesson.
screen: `GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.` → `A POT RISING ON THE WHEEL.` → `SOMETHING GOES WRONG.`

segments.voice: Here's what Jeremiah sees. "And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it." He doesn't throw the clay out, or sweep it off the wheel into the trash. The spoiled pot is still soft clay, and soft clay can be pressed back down and raised again into something else. Then the word comes. "O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter?" And: "Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand." On its own, that could sound like a threat: you're just clay, and I can crush you. But read on. God says that if a nation he has spoken against turns from its evil, he will relent of the evil he planned for it. And if a nation he planned to build turns to evil, the plan can change too. The potter image is about turning. A vessel still on the wheel isn't finished; mistakes don't end it, they're the reason the potter's hands go back to work. Jewish tradition carries this picture into Yom Kippur. In the Ashkenazi evening service, a liturgical poem built on Jeremiah's image is sung: behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are we in your hand. On the night of turning, the people call themselves clay that can still be reshaped.
screen: `THE VESSEL WAS MARRED.` · `HE MADE IT AGAIN.` · then, large: `AS CLAY IN THE POTTER'S HAND.` · then: `CLAY ON THE WHEEL CAN TURN.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one place that feels marred, a habit that slumped, a plan that caved in, a way you've been treating someone, and hold it the way a potter holds soft clay, without throwing it away or defending it. Ask what it could become if it were pressed down and raised again. Then let your hands, your shoulders, your jaw go soft, like clay that can still move.
Yom Kippur, the night of turning, when a liturgical poem sung in the Ashkenazi evening service borrows Jeremiah's image: as clay in the hand of the potter, so are we in your hand. Today's word.

803.title: Fire in my bones (Jeremiah 20:7–9)
803.hook: Jeremiah tries to stop speaking, but the word is "as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones"
803.carry: silence turned out to be impossible
803.tomorrow: Seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:4–7)
803.howItsDone: Jews read Jeremiah's complaints, like this one in chapter 20, as part of the prophetic books; arguing with God, from Abraham to Job to Jeremiah, has a recognized place in Jewish prayer and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a spoiled pot was pressed down and made again, the image sung on Yom Kippur: as clay in his hand. Today, the prophet tries to quit.

Jeremiah has a bad night. Pashhur, a priest and an officer in the Temple, hears him prophesying disaster, has him struck, and locks him overnight in the stocks at the upper gate of Benjamin, by the house of the Lord. The next morning Pashhur lets him out, and Jeremiah speaks one more hard word to him. Then the book opens the door to Jeremiah's private prayer, and what comes out is a complaint against God.
screen: `A NIGHT IN THE STOCKS.` → `ONE MORE HARD WORD.` → `A COMPLAINT AGAINST GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's how it starts. "O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me." The Hebrew verb behind deceived can also mean persuaded or enticed, and translators wrestle with how strong to make it. Either way, Jeremiah is saying: you talked me into this, and I lost. Every time I open my mouth it's violence and ruin, and every time, I'm laughed at. So he decides to stop. "Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name." And here's what happens. "But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay." Holding it in wears him out more than the mockery did. The word won't stay buried. Two things are worth keeping. First, the book keeps this prayer. It doesn't tidy Jeremiah into a calm saint. Jewish tradition has room for arguing with God: Abraham bargains over Sodom, Job demands an answer, and here a prophet says, you tricked me. Second, the fire isn't a reward or a glow of inspiration. It's a pressure. Some truths, once you know them, cost more to keep silent than to say. Jeremiah's lesson isn't that speaking got easier. It's that silence turned out to be impossible.
screen: `THOU HAST DECEIVED ME.` · `I WILL NOT SPEAK ANY MORE.` · then, large: `A BURNING FIRE SHUT UP IN MY BONES.` · then: `SILENCE COSTS MORE.`

segments.voice: Ask yourself whether there's something you keep swallowing: a truth someone needs to hear, an apology you owe, a worry about someone you love. Put it into one clear sentence in your head, kind and true, without speaking it to anyone yet. If the sentence comes out angry, breathe and try again until it's honest without being cruel.
Pashhur, the priest who struck Jeremiah and locked him in the stocks overnight, only to hear one more hard word the next morning. Today's word.
Your line: silence turned out to be impossible. Even a prophet's complaint made it into the book. Until tomorrow.

804.title: Seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:4–7)
804.hook: a letter to the exiles: build houses, plant gardens, pray for the city you live in
804.carry: plant a garden there, and pray for the place
804.howItsDone: In synagogue, a prayer for the welfare of the country and its government is said on Shabbat morning after the Torah reading, carrying forward Jeremiah's instruction to seek the peace of the city.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah tried to keep quiet, and the word burned in his bones: silence turned out to be impossible. Today, the prophet speaks by letter, to people far away.

A letter goes out from Jerusalem, carried by messengers, to people who have been taken away to Babylon: elders, priests, prophets, craftsmen, ordinary families. They're living in the capital of the empire that conquered them. And some prophets among them are saying: don't unpack. This will be over soon. Jeremiah's letter says something else, and to people who wanted to hear go home, it is a hard letter.
screen: `A LETTER TO BABYLON.` → `DON'T UNPACK, SOME SAY.` → `JEREMIAH SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the heart of it. "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them." Houses are for staying. Gardens take time to bear. Jeremiah is telling the exiles to stop waiting at the door. Marry, he goes on, have children, see your children married, increase there and don't dwindle. Then the line that gives today its title. "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." The city is Babylon, the power that conquered Jerusalem. And the exiles are told to seek its shalom, its peace, its welfare, and to pray for it. Not because Babylon deserves it, but because their lives are now tied to it: in its peace, your peace. Later in the chapter the letter promises a return, but not soon. Until then, live fully where you are. A related teaching appears in the Mishnah. Pirkei Avot records Rabbi Chanina, the deputy high priest, saying: pray for the welfare of the government, for without fear of it, people would swallow one another alive. And synagogue prayer books include a prayer for the country and its government, said on Shabbat. Jeremiah's letter asked something hard of people living somewhere they never chose: plant a garden there, and pray for the place.
screen: `BUILD HOUSES, PLANT GARDENS.` · then, large: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · then: `IN ITS PEACE, YOUR PEACE.` · `PRAY FOR THE WELFARE OF THE GOVERNMENT.`

segments.voice: Bring your town or city to mind, the actual streets, and pick one place: the bus stop, the corner store, the school, the clinic, the park. Think of the people who work there and the people who need it, and ask what its peace needs right now. If you pray, you can hold Jeremiah's words for it; if you don't, hold the wish.
shalom, the peace Jeremiah told the exiles to seek for Babylon, the city that conquered them, and to pray for: for in its peace is yours. Today's word.

805.title: Rachel weeping (Jeremiah 31:14–16)
805.hook: Rachel weeps for her children, and is told "there is hope for thy future"
805.howItsDone: These verses come near the end of the haftarah read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and people come to pray at the site known as Rachel's Tomb, near Bethlehem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a letter told the exiles to seek the shalom of Babylon, to plant gardens and pray for the place. Today, from the chapters of comfort, a mother's voice.
screen: `PLANT A GARDEN THERE, AND PRAY FOR THE PLACE.`

segments.voice: "A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Rachel. Jacob's beloved, the wife he waited and worked for. She died on the road, giving birth to a son, and Genesis says she was buried there, in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Generations later, Jeremiah hears her voice again. Her children are being led away into exile, and she is weeping.
screen: `A VOICE WAS HEARD IN RAMAH.` → `BURIED ON THE ROAD.` → `SHE REFUSES TO BE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Notice first what Rachel refuses: comfort. Not because comfort is bad, but because her children are gone, and nothing short of their return will do. The text lets her grief stand at full height. Then God answers, and he doesn't tell her she's overreacting. "Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD; and they shall come again from the land of the enemy." Thy work. Her weeping is called work, labor that will be paid. And then: "And there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border." The Jewish Publication Society's old translation puts it this way: "there is hope for thy future." Rabbinic tradition built on this. The commentator Rashi explains why Jacob buried Rachel on the road instead of in the family tomb: so that when her children were driven into exile, they would pass her grave, and she would come out and weep and plead for them. And a midrash in Lamentations Rabbah tells that when the Temple fell, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Moses each pleaded for the people, and were not answered. Then Rachel spoke, and God said: for your sake I will bring them back. The one who refused comfort is the one whose tears are heard. Hope here isn't the opposite of grief. It's what God says to grief that refuses to quit.
screen: `SHE REFUSES TO BE COMFORTED.` · `THY WORK SHALL BE REWARDED.` · then, large: `THERE IS HOPE FOR THY FUTURE.` · then: `RACHEL'S TEARS ARE HEARD.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who seems far away right now, lost to addiction, to anger, to grief, to a life that's drifted from yours, and don't argue with how hard it is; Rachel didn't. Let yourself care about them without pretending, and quietly set Jeremiah's words next to their name: there is hope. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer.
Rachel weeping. The mother of the exiles, crying for her children and refusing comfort, and told: there is hope for thy future. Today's word.
Your line: there is hope. Her tears were called work, and they were heard. See you tomorrow.
